questions.q: Identify the grammatical category of the word "Hklh.k" as used in the opening line "dey iwQyrsA Hkkst eas ¯gnqvksa osQ ;gk¡ Hkkstu dey&i=k ij ijkslk tkrkA dey&i=k dks iqjbu dgrsA dey osQ uky dks Hklh.k dgrsA". Explain its morphological composition.
questions.a: "Hklh.k" is a masculine singular noun in the direct case, formed from the root "Hklh" (to carry/lift) + the nominalizing suffix "-k" (krdant), meaning "that which is carried/lifted" — here, the edible kernel of the dey fruit. A wrong answer (e.g., calling it a verb or adjective) reveals the student cannot distinguish derivational morphology (krdant formation) from inflectional verb forms, a core gap for analyzing dialectal nominalizations in the text.

questions.q: The text uses "oqQeqn" as a synonym for "tyiq"i". Explain the semantic nuance that makes "oqQeqn" the preferred term in the village context, and identify the grammatical feature that signals this is a dialect borrowing rather than standard Hindi.
questions.a: "oqQeqn" (from Avadhi/Braj "oqQe" = water/liquid + "qn" = particle) specifically denotes the watery pulp surrounding the seed, carrying sensory immediacy — the villager experiences the fruit as juice-first. The final nasalized "-n" (anunasik) in "oqQeqn" is the grammatical marker of its dialect origin; standard Hindi would use "oqQb;k¡" or "tyiq"i". A student who misses the anunasik as a dialect marker treats the word as mere vocabulary, not as grammatical evidence of the text's linguistic landscape.

questions.q: In the sentence "fclukFk cgqr fnuksa le>rs Fks fd dksb;k¡ flI+kZQ gekjs ;gk¡ dk iwQy gSA", identify the tense-aspect combination of "le>rs Fks" and explain why the author chooses this over simple past "le>k Fks" or perfective "le>k x;k".
questions.a: "le>rs Fks" is habitual past (imperfective) — "used to understand/kept understanding". The author chooses it to convey a prolonged, repeated state of belief over "cgqr fnuksa" (many days), contrasting with the sudden revelation that follows. Simple past "le>k Fks" would imply a single completed act of understanding; perfective "le>k x;k" would emphasize resultative completion. A student who selects the wrong tense-aspect misses how aspect encodes duration and epistemological stance — a recurring pattern in the memoir's narration of childhood perception.

questions.q: Compare the honorific systems operating in these two passages: (a) "fclukFk dks mUgksaus gh ikyk&ikslkA" and (b) "ek¡ us ”kksj ls FkIiM+ ekjk fiQj ikl esa cSBh ukmu ls dgkµnk¡r fudkys gS] Vhlr gSA". Analyze how pronoun choice and verb agreement encode shifting power dynamics.
questions.a: In (a), "mUgksaus" (ergative plural honorific) + "ikyk&ikslk" (plural verb agreement) shows the villagers collectively addressing Chhutki with respect due to her father's status — third-person plural honorific for a child. In (b), mother uses "ukmu" (familiar singular "you") + "fudkys" (singular verb) with the child, but the reported speech "nk¡r fudkyrs gSa" shifts to plural "gSa" when the child addresses the father ("gj ph”k"), reflecting the child's internalized honorific code. A student who sees only "politeness" misses the grammatical mapping of social hierarchy: ergative subject + plural verb = institutional respect; familiar pronoun + singular verb = intimacy; plural verb in reported speech = performed deference.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The dense clustering of onomatopoeic words (e.g., 'rsy&rsy', 'f[kys f[kys', 'djsyk', 'fephZ') in the 'iwQy f[kys' passage functions primarily as decorative sound-play." Support or refute with grammatical evidence.
questions.a: Refute. Grammatically, these are not mere nouns/adjectives but **echo-form reduplicatives** (dvandva/echo compounds) functioning as **adverbial manner modifiers** of the verb "f[kys" (resound/ring). "rsy&rsy" (reduplicated stem) + "f[kys f[kys" (iterative verb) + "djsyk" (onomatopoeic adverb) + "fephZ" (echo-word) create a syntactic chain where each layer intensifies the sensory duration: reduplication → iterative aspect → manner adverb → echo-word. This is grammatical iconicity — form mimicking the unending, layered soundscape. A student calling it "decoration" misses that reduplication and iteration are grammatical categories in Hindi, not stylistic flourishes.

questions.q: Rewrite the sentence "iwQy f[kys] f[kys iwQy / èkku iwQy] dksnks iwQy / oqQVdh iwQy f[kysA" as a standard Hindi prose sentence using finite verbs, then explain what is lost in translation.
questions.a: Standard Hindi: "iwQy bajti hain, baar-baar bajti hain; èkku ki awaz hai, dhool ki awaz hai, barish ki awaz bajti hai." Lost: (1) **Nominal predicate structure** — "iwQy f[kys" treats sound as noun+verb complex, not subject+finite verb; (2) **Elliptical parallelism** — each line drops the verb, creating rhythmic equivalence across sound-types; (3) **Present-habitual fusion** — "f[kys" (singular verb with plural sense) merges timeless truth with immediate perception; (4) **Oral prosody** — the slash-separated fragments mirror breath-units of folk singing. A student who produces only the prose version cannot articulate how grammar *is* the poem's rhythm.
